cards.q: What are the three steps of the cycle the CPU repeats?
cards.a: Fetch, decode, execute. Fetch copies the instruction the program counter points at into the CPU and moves the program counter on. Decode works out what that number means. Execute does it.
cards.lessonTitle: What Happens When a Program Runs

cards.q: What is the difference between memory and storage?
cards.a: Memory (RAM) holds the program that is running and the values it is working with, and it is emptied when the power goes off. Storage keeps files for the long term. A program file has to be copied from storage into memory before it can run.
cards.lessonTitle: What Happens When a Program Runs

cards.q: What is a register?
cards.a: A small, very fast storage slot inside the CPU itself. Arithmetic happens in registers; values are copied in from memory first and copied back afterwards.
cards.lessonTitle: What Happens When a Program Runs

cards.q: Why can a debugger show you every value in a running program?
cards.a: Because the CPU does one instruction at a time, a tool can pause it between two instructions. At that moment every register and every memory cell holds a definite number that can be read.
cards.lessonTitle: What Happens When a Program Runs

cards.q: How many different values can one byte hold, and why?
cards.a: 256. A byte is eight bits, each bit doubles the number of combinations, and 2 multiplied by itself eight times is 256. Unsigned, that is 0 to 255.

cards.q: Why does one hexadecimal digit correspond to exactly four bits?
cards.a: Because sixteen is two to the power of four. Four bits can form sixteen combinations, and hexadecimal has sixteen digits, so each digit matches one combination.

cards.q: How do you negate a number in two's complement?
cards.a: Flip every bit, then add one. For example 5 is `0000 0101`; flipped it is `1111 1010`; add one and it is `1111 1011`, which is -5.

cards.q: What does "little-endian" mean?
cards.a: When a value takes several bytes, the lowest-value byte is stored at the lowest address. The `int` 1000, which is `0x000003E8`, sits in memory as `E8 03 00 00`.

cards.q: What happens when an unsigned value goes past its largest value?
cards.a: It wraps round to zero and carries on from there. Nothing reports an error. For signed types the result is undefined behaviour, which is worse.

cards.q: What is the difference between `p`, `*p` and `&p`?
cards.a: `p` is the address the pointer holds. `*p` is the value stored at that address. `&p` is the address of the pointer variable itself, since a pointer is a variable and has to live somewhere too.

cards.q: Why does adding one to an `int*` move it by four bytes?
cards.a: Pointer arithmetic counts in elements, not bytes. The compiler multiplies by the size of the type pointed at, so `p + 1` is the address of the next `int`, which is four bytes on.

cards.q: What is padding, and why does the compiler add it?
cards.a: Padding is unused bytes placed between variables or struct members. It keeps each value at an address that is a multiple of its size, because the processor reads aligned values fastest.

cards.q: Why is dereferencing `nullptr` a crash, and why is that a good thing?
cards.a: The operating system guarantees nothing lives at address 0, so any attempt to read or write there is stopped as an access violation. It is useful because the program fails immediately at the faulty line instead of silently corrupting memory.

cards.q: Why are memory locations often described as a base plus an offset?
cards.a: Absolute addresses change from one run to the next. The distance from the start of a struct, or from the start of a loaded program, to a particular value does not. Finding the base at run time and adding a fixed offset works every time.

cards.q: Name the four stages of a build, in order.
cards.a: Preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker. The first three run once per `.cpp` file; the linker runs once for the whole program.
cards.lessonTitle: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code

cards.q: Why is each `.cpp` file compiled separately?
cards.a: So that changing one file only means recompiling that one file. The linker then joins the pieces. It also means one file cannot see another's definitions, only the declarations it includes.
cards.lessonTitle: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code

cards.q: What is the difference between a compiler error and a linker error?
cards.a: A compiler error means the code in one file is not valid C++. A linker error means every file was valid on its own, but the pieces do not fit together: something is missing or defined twice.
cards.lessonTitle: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code

cards.q: What does `.pdb` stand for in Visual Studio, and what is it for?
cards.a: Program database. It holds the debug symbols: which machine code came from which source line, and the names and types of variables. The debugger needs it to show you your own code instead of raw instructions.
cards.lessonTitle: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code

cards.q: What is a stack frame?
cards.a: The block of stack memory set aside for one call of a function. It holds the return address, the function's locals and some bookkeeping, and is released when the call returns.
cards.lessonTitle: Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look

cards.q: What does the `rsp` register hold?
cards.a: The address of the current top of the stack, which is its lowest address in use. Making room on the stack means subtracting from `rsp`.
cards.lessonTitle: Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look

cards.q: Why is returning `&localVariable` a bug?
cards.a: The local lives in the function's frame, and the frame is released when the function returns. The caller is left with the address of memory that will soon be reused for something else.
cards.lessonTitle: Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look

cards.q: What causes a stack overflow?
cards.a: Using more stack than was reserved for it: usually recursion that never stops, or very large local variables.
cards.lessonTitle: Function Calls and the Stack: A First Look

cards.q: What is the difference between user mode and kernel mode?
cards.a: Kernel mode has full control of the hardware and all memory. User mode, where normal programs run, is restricted and has to ask the kernel through system calls for anything outside its own process.
cards.lessonTitle: What the Operating System Does for a Program

cards.q: What does the Windows loader do when a program starts?
cards.a: It creates a process, maps the program's code and data into its address space, loads the DLLs it needs and fills in the addresses of the functions it uses from them, then starts the first thread.
cards.lessonTitle: What the Operating System Does for a Program

cards.q: What is a handle?
cards.a: A small number a process uses to refer to a kernel object it has opened, such as a file, thread or event. The kernel checks every use of it against the process's rights.
cards.lessonTitle: What the Operating System Does for a Program

cards.q: Why can one process not simply read another process's variables through a pointer?
cards.a: Each process has its own virtual address space. An address only has meaning inside the process it came from.
cards.lessonTitle: What the Operating System Does for a Program

cards.q: What is the difference between a project and a solution?
cards.a: A project builds one program or library from its source files. A solution is a container for one or more related projects.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up Visual Studio for This Course

cards.q: Name two ways a Debug build differs from a Release build.
cards.a: Debug has optimisation turned off, so the code follows the source line by line, and adds checks such as filling uninitialised memory with `0xCC`. Release is optimised: faster, but harder to follow in a debugger.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up Visual Studio for This Course

cards.q: Where does Visual Studio put the program it builds?
cards.a: In a folder named after the platform and configuration, such as `x64\Debug\`, next to its `.pdb` debug symbols.
cards.lessonTitle: Setting Up Visual Studio for This Course

cards.q: What does a breakpoint do?
cards.a: It makes the debugger pause the program just before that line runs, so you can inspect its state.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change

cards.q: What is the difference between Step Over and Step Into?
cards.a: Step Over (F10) runs the whole current line, including any calls, and stops at the next line. Step Into (F11) goes into the function the line calls and stops at its first line.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change

cards.q: How do you see the raw bytes of a variable?
cards.a: Open the Memory window (Debug → Windows → Memory) and type the variable's address, such as `&hero`, into the Address box.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change

cards.q: What does the Call Stack window show?
cards.a: The chain of function calls that led to the current line, newest at the top. Each entry is one stack frame, and double-clicking it shows that frame's locals.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First Debugging Session: Watching Memory Change

cards.q: List the parts of an x64 Windows stack frame, from the caller's side down.
cards.a: Shadow space reserved by the caller, the return address pushed by `call`, registers the function saves, its locals, and space for the calls it makes itself.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses

cards.q: Why are frame sizes often 8 more than you would expect?
cards.a: The `call` pushed an 8-byte return address, leaving `rsp` 8 off a multiple of 16. The function adds 8 to its frame to bring it back into alignment for its own calls.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses

cards.q: How do you turn a recursive search into one that cannot overflow the stack?
cards.a: Put the work still to do (cells, nodes, positions) into a container such as `std::vector` used as a stack, and loop: take one item out, process it, push its neighbours, until the container is empty.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses

cards.q: Name two reasons to put data on the heap instead of the stack.
cards.a: Its size is only known at run time, or it must outlive the function that created it. Very large data also belongs on the heap because the stack is small.
cards.lessonTitle: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time

cards.q: What is a memory leak?
cards.a: Heap memory that is never freed after the program has finished with it. The memory stays reserved until the process ends.
cards.lessonTitle: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time

cards.q: What do the Debug heap patterns `CD`, `DD` and `FD` mean?
cards.a: `CD` is allocated but not yet written, `DD` is freed, and `FD` is the guard area around each block that detects writes past its ends.
cards.lessonTitle: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time

cards.q: What is an arena allocator?
cards.a: One large block of memory from which pieces are handed out by simply moving an offset forward. Individual pieces are never freed; the whole block is reset at once, for example at the end of a frame or a level.
cards.lessonTitle: The Heap: Asking for Memory at Run Time

cards.q: What are the three storage durations, and where does each one's memory come from?
cards.a: Automatic (the stack), dynamic (the heap) and static (the program's image, laid out by the linker and mapped in by the loader).
cards.lessonTitle: Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory

cards.q: What is the difference between `.data` and `.rdata`?
cards.a: `.data` holds writable globals and statics that start with a value. `.rdata` holds read-only data such as string literals and constants, and writing to it crashes.
cards.lessonTitle: Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory

cards.q: How does a function with a `static` local avoid initialisation-order problems?
cards.a: The local is initialised the first time the function is called, so it is always ready by the time anything uses it, whatever order the program's globals were set up in.
cards.lessonTitle: Static Storage and the Layout of a Program in Memory

cards.q: When does an object's lifetime begin and end?
cards.a: It begins when its constructor finishes and ends when its destructor starts. Outside that window, using it is undefined behaviour even if its memory still exists.
cards.lessonTitle: Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid

cards.q: Why is `const char* p = makeString().c_str();` a bug?
cards.a: The `std::string` returned by `makeString` is a temporary destroyed at the end of the line. `p` then points into memory the string has freed.
cards.lessonTitle: Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid

cards.q: Name three kinds of resource that RAII can manage.
cards.a: Heap memory, open files, locks, Windows handles, or any "undo this when finished" action.
cards.lessonTitle: Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid

cards.q: State the three layout rules for a struct.
cards.a: Each member starts at a multiple of its own alignment; the struct's alignment is its largest member alignment; its size is rounded up to a multiple of that alignment.

cards.q: How do you usually reduce a struct's padding?
cards.a: Declare the members in order of decreasing alignment: 8-byte members first, then 4, 2 and 1.

cards.q: Why should structs with padding not be compared with `memcmp`?
cards.a: The padding bytes are not initialised to anything in particular, so two structs with equal members can still have different bytes in their padding.

cards.q: Which parts of a class take up space in each object?
cards.a: The non-static data members, laid out with padding, plus a hidden vptr if the class has virtual functions. Member functions, static members and access specifiers do not.
cards.lessonTitle: How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out

cards.q: Why can a `Monster*` be used as an `Entity*` without changing the address?
cards.a: With single inheritance the `Entity` subobject is at offset 0 of the `Monster`, so both pointers refer to the same address.
cards.lessonTitle: How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out

cards.q: What is `this`?
cards.a: A hidden argument to every non-static member function, holding the address of the object the function was called on.
cards.lessonTitle: How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out

cards.q: How is the address of `a[i]` worked out?
cards.a: The address of `a[0]` plus `i` times the size of one element.
cards.lessonTitle: Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory

cards.q: What does row-major order mean?
cards.a: A two-dimensional array is stored one complete row after another, so the element at (row, column) is at index row × width + column.
cards.lessonTitle: Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory

cards.q: Why does loop order affect speed over a big grid?
cards.a: Memory is fetched in 64-byte cache lines. Walking along a row uses every byte of each line; walking down a column jumps a whole row each step and fetches a new line nearly every time.
cards.lessonTitle: Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory

cards.q: How does `strlen` find the length of a C string?
cards.a: It walks along from the first character, counting, until it finds the zero byte that ends the string.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings

cards.q: What is the small string optimisation?
cards.a: Storing short strings directly inside the `std::string` object instead of in a separate heap block, so they need no allocation. On MSVC, up to 15 characters.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings

cards.q: What is the difference between UTF-8 and UTF-16?
cards.a: Both encode Unicode. UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes per character and matches ASCII for English text. UTF-16 uses 2 or 4 bytes per character; Windows uses it internally and for `wchar_t`.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings

cards.q: Why are memory bugs harder to find than logic bugs?
cards.a: The symptom often appears far from the cause, at a different time, or only in some builds, because the bug corrupts whatever happens to be nearby in memory.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks

cards.q: What is the difference between a dangling pointer and a leak?
cards.a: A dangling pointer refers to memory that has been freed or whose object has ended. A leak is memory that is still allocated but that nothing refers to or will ever free.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks

cards.q: How do ids or handles help avoid use-after-free bugs?
cards.a: Instead of keeping a pointer to an object that might be destroyed, code keeps an id and looks the object up when it needs it. If the object is gone, the lookup fails safely instead of reaching freed memory.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks

cards.q: How does AddressSanitizer know an access is invalid?
cards.a: It surrounds every allocation with forbidden red zones, marks freed memory forbidden, records all of this in shadow memory, and checks the shadow before every load and store.

cards.q: What three locations can an ASan use-after-free report give you?
cards.a: Where the bad access happened, where the memory was freed, and where it was originally allocated.

cards.q: Why keep a separate ASan build configuration?
cards.a: ASan slows the program down and is incompatible with some options such as Edit and Continue, so it is best switched on in its own configuration and run regularly, while normal debugging stays fast.

cards.q: How can you tell a pointer from other data in the Memory window?
cards.a: It is 8 bytes, usually 8-byte aligned, and ends in `00 00` with repeating high bytes, such as `f6 7f 00 00` for the program's own image.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio

cards.q: What are the three parts of a 32-bit float?
cards.a: One sign bit, an 8-bit exponent stored with a bias of 127, and a 23-bit fraction.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio

cards.q: What steps decode an unknown object in memory?
cards.a: Work out the member offsets from the type and alignment rules, point the window at the object, split the bytes by offset, read each member with the right rule (integer, float, pointer, padding), and check against the Locals window.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio

cards.q: What does a pointer to a pointer hold?
cards.a: The address of another pointer variable.

cards.q: Give two common reasons to use a pointer to a pointer.
cards.a: To let a function change which object the caller's pointer points at (an out parameter), and to work with arrays of pointers such as `argv`.

cards.q: How many bytes does `argv + 1` move on x64?
cards.a: Eight: one pointer. Pointer arithmetic moves by the size of the thing pointed at, and `argv` points at pointers.

cards.q: What two steps does following `p->member` take?
cards.a: Read the address held in `p`, then access the bytes at that address plus the member's offset.

cards.q: How can you tell from a crash address that a null pointer was followed?
cards.a: The address is small, equal to the offset of the member that was being read from address zero.

cards.q: Name two ways games reduce pointer chasing.
cards.a: Storing objects by value inside their owners, keeping objects in arrays rather than arrays of pointers, and referring to them by index or handle.

cards.q: How is a reference parameter passed at the machine level?
cards.a: As an address, exactly like a pointer.

cards.q: Why are references safer than pointers?
cards.a: They cannot be null, cannot be re-aimed at a different object, and need no `*` or `->`, which removes several common mistakes.

cards.q: When should you still use a pointer instead of a reference?
cards.a: When the object might be absent (null), when what is referred to must be able to change, or when you need to store it in a container or an assignable class.

cards.q: What is the difference in machine code between a direct call and a call through a function pointer?
cards.a: A direct call jumps to an address fixed when the program was linked. A call through a pointer reads the address from a register or memory at run time and jumps there.

cards.q: What is a callback?
cards.a: A function passed to other code so that the other code can call it when needed, letting the caller decide part of the behaviour.

cards.q: When would you choose `std::function` over a plain function pointer?
cards.a: When the callable needs to carry data, such as a lambda with captures, and must be stored for later.

cards.q: What is a vtable?
cards.a: A per-class array of function pointers, one slot per virtual function, which objects use to find the right function at run time.
cards.lessonTitle: Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory

cards.q: Why does every class put a given virtual function in the same slot?
cards.a: So that code holding only a base pointer can call it by slot number, without knowing the object's real class.
cards.lessonTitle: Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory

cards.q: What does a virtual call cost compared with a normal call?
cards.a: Two extra dependent memory reads (the vptr and the table entry), an indirect call, and usually no inlining.
cards.lessonTitle: Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory

cards.q: What does each node of a singly linked list hold?
cards.a: An element's value and a pointer to the next node, or `nullptr` in the last node.

cards.q: Why is inserting at the front of a list cheap?
cards.a: It only creates one node and changes two pointers, whatever the list's length; nothing has to move.

cards.q: Give two situations where games use linked structures sensibly.
cards.a: Intrusive lists, where the link lives inside objects that already exist (such as the objects in one cell of a spatial grid), and free lists in object pools.

cards.q: What three pointers make up a `std::vector`, and how are size and capacity worked out?
cards.a: The start of the block, the end of the elements in use, and the end of the block. Size is used end minus start; capacity is block end minus start.

cards.q: Why can a pointer to a vector element become invalid after `push_back`?
cards.a: If the vector is full, `push_back` moves every element to a new block and frees the old one, so the pointer refers to freed memory.

cards.q: When is swap-and-pop the right way to remove an element?
cards.a: When the order of the elements does not matter: it removes in constant time by moving the last element into the gap.

cards.q: What two properties should a hash function have?
cards.a: It must always give the same hash for the same key, and it should spread keys evenly, so that similar keys give very different hashes.

cards.q: What is the load factor, and why does it matter?
cards.a: The number of entries divided by the number of buckets. A high load factor means more collisions and slower lookups, so tables grow and rehash when it passes a limit.

cards.q: When would you choose `std::map` over `std::unordered_map`?
cards.a: When you need the keys in sorted order, or need to find the entries just before or after a key.

cards.q: What is a scene graph, and why do positions in it add up on the way down?
cards.a: A tree of game objects attached to one another. Each node's position is relative to its parent, so its world position is its parent's world position plus its own.

cards.q: What is the difference between depth-first and breadth-first search?
cards.a: Depth-first goes as deep as it can down one branch before backing up, using a stack; breadth-first visits everything one step away, then two steps, and so on, using a queue.

cards.q: How do you recover the actual path, not just its length, from a BFS?
cards.a: Record, for each place, the place it was reached from; then follow those records back from the target to the start.

cards.q: What three things does a container of game objects usually need to do well?
cards.a: Loop quickly over the live objects, add and remove them cheaply, and let other code refer to an object safely.
cards.lessonTitle: Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools

cards.q: How does a generational handle detect that its object is gone?
cards.a: Each slot's generation increases when it is freed. The handle stores the generation from when it was made; if the slot's current generation differs, the object has been destroyed.
cards.lessonTitle: Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools

cards.q: Why are handles safer to store than pointers?
cards.a: A stale pointer silently reaches freed or reused memory. A stale handle is detected on lookup and returns nothing.
cards.lessonTitle: Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools

cards.q: What is the difference between a solution and a project?
cards.a: A project builds one output (an exe, dll or lib) from its sources and settings. A solution groups related projects and records which to build in which configuration.

cards.q: Why might a setting work in Debug but not in Release?
cards.a: Each configuration and platform has its own complete set of settings, so a change made with only Debug selected does not apply to Release.

cards.q: What is a property sheet for?
cards.a: Holding settings shared by several projects, so they are set once and stay consistent.

cards.q: What does the one definition rule require?
cards.a: Each used function and variable must be defined exactly once in the program; classes, templates and inline functions may be defined in several translation units only if every definition is identical.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What

cards.q: Why do class definitions go in headers but function bodies usually do not?
cards.a: Classes may be defined in every translation unit that needs them (identically); ordinary functions must be defined only once, so their bodies go in one `.cpp` file.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What

cards.q: What is name mangling?
cards.a: The compiler's encoding of a function's full identity (namespace, class, parameter types) into a single symbol name, so that overloads and members get distinct symbols for the linker.
cards.lessonTitle: Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What

cards.q: Why fix the first error first?
cards.a: Later errors are often consequences of the compiler misreading the code after the first mistake; fixing it frequently clears the rest.

cards.q: How can you tell a compiler error from a linker error?
cards.a: Compiler errors have codes starting with `C`; linker errors start with `LNK`. Linker errors only appear once every file has compiled.

cards.q: What does C2664 usually tell you, and what should you read in it?
cards.a: An argument has the wrong type. Read the "from X to Y" types carefully, comparing const-ness, pointers and references.

cards.q: How does the linker decide which parts of a static library go into the program?
cards.a: It copies in each object file from the library that defines a symbol the program still needs, repeating until nothing more is needed.

cards.q: Why must a library be built with the same runtime library and configuration as the program?
cards.a: Object files built with different runtime libraries or Debug/Release settings can disagree about the C runtime and about the layout of standard types, which causes link errors or crashes.

cards.q: When would you choose a DLL over a static library?
cards.a: When the code must be loaded or replaced at run time, as with plugins, or shared between several programs as one file.

cards.q: What are the two ways a program can use a DLL?
cards.a: Load-time linking, through an import library, where the loader resolves the DLL when the program starts; and run-time loading, with `LoadLibrary` and `GetProcAddress`, where the program loads it and looks functions up itself.
cards.lessonTitle: Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL

cards.q: Why should only simple C types cross a DLL boundary?
cards.a: The DLL and the program may be built with different compilers or settings, so standard library types may have different layouts or use different heaps on each side.
cards.lessonTitle: Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL

cards.q: What does `GetProcAddress` return, and what must you do with it?
cards.a: The address of an exported function (or null). You cast it to a function pointer of exactly the right signature before calling it.
cards.lessonTitle: Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL

cards.q: What three jobs does vcpkg do for each dependency?
cards.a: It downloads the library's source, builds it to match the project's platform and runtime (the triplet), and connects the headers, libraries and DLLs to the project.

cards.q: What does manifest mode mean?
cards.a: The project's dependencies are listed in a `vcpkg.json` file kept with the project, and vcpkg installs them automatically when the project is built.

cards.q: Which files from vcpkg belong in version control?
cards.a: `vcpkg.json` (and `vcpkg-configuration.json` if present), not the `vcpkg_installed` build output.

cards.q: How does Windows involve the debugger when a breakpoint is hit?
cards.a: The `int 3` instruction raises a breakpoint exception; because a debugger is attached to the process, Windows delivers the event to the debugger instead of to the program.
cards.lessonTitle: The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack

cards.q: How do you find out why a function was called with a bad argument?
cards.a: In the Call Stack window, double-click the caller's frame and look at its variables in Locals and Watch.
cards.lessonTitle: The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack

cards.q: Why attach to a process instead of starting it in the debugger?
cards.a: When the problem only appears after the program has run for a while, when another program starts it, or when you do not want to restart it.
cards.lessonTitle: The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack

cards.q: What are format specifiers for?
cards.a: Changing how the Watch window shows a value: as hex or binary, as an array of N elements, as a string, as an error message, and so on.
cards.lessonTitle: Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows

cards.q: Which registers hold the first four integer arguments on x64 Windows, and which the return value?
cards.a: RCX, RDX, R8 and R9 for the arguments; RAX for the return value.
cards.lessonTitle: Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows

cards.q: What does the Disassembly window show?
cards.a: The machine instructions the compiler generated, with their addresses and optionally their bytes, interleaved with the source lines they came from.
cards.lessonTitle: Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows

cards.q: What is the difference between a breakpoint and a data breakpoint?
cards.a: A breakpoint stops when execution reaches a line of code. A data breakpoint stops when a particular address in memory is written (or read), whatever code does it.

cards.q: What are the hardware limits on data breakpoints?
cards.a: Four at a time, each covering 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes at an address aligned to that size.

cards.q: How would you find the code that writes past the end of a heap block?
cards.a: Find the block (for example with `_CrtSetBreakAlloc`), then set a data breakpoint on the bytes just after its end; the debugger stops on the instruction that writes there.

cards.q: What is the as-if rule?
cards.a: The compiler may transform the program in any way that does not change its observable behaviour, as long as the program has no undefined behaviour.
cards.lessonTitle: Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes

cards.q: Name four things the optimiser does.
cards.a: Keeps variables in registers, inlines functions, folds constants, removes dead code, transforms and vectorises loops, reorders instructions.
cards.lessonTitle: Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes

cards.q: How do you make a Release build debuggable without slowing it down?
cards.a: Generate debug information (`/Zi` and the linker's debug info option), which writes a separate `.pdb` and does not change the code; use `#pragma optimize("", off)` around a function that needs closer inspection.
cards.lessonTitle: Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes

cards.q: Why does Windows give programs handles instead of pointers to kernel objects?
cards.a: Kernel objects live in kernel memory, which user-mode code cannot access; a handle lets the kernel look the object up and check the process's rights each time it is used.

cards.q: What happens to a process's open handles when it exits?
cards.a: Windows closes them all, and any object whose last handle that was is destroyed.

cards.q: Why does the `UniqueHandle` class treat both `nullptr` and `INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE` as empty?
cards.a: Different Windows functions use different values to mean failure, so checking for both makes the class safe whatever produced the handle.

cards.q: Name the three main ways Windows API functions report failure.
cards.a: A `BOOL` returning `FALSE`; a null or invalid handle; an `HRESULT` with its severity bit set. The first two use `GetLastError` for the reason.
cards.lessonTitle: Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation

cards.q: What are the three fields of an HRESULT?
cards.a: Severity (failure or success), facility (which subsystem), and the code within that facility.
cards.lessonTitle: Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation

cards.q: What is the two-call pattern?
cards.a: Calling a function first to learn how big a buffer its result needs, then allocating a buffer of that size and calling it again.
cards.lessonTitle: Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation

cards.q: Which of the A and W versions does Windows implement natively, and why does it matter?
cards.a: The W (UTF-16) versions. The A versions convert through the current code page, which loses any character that code page cannot represent.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8

cards.q: What is the usual strategy for text in a Windows program?
cards.a: Keep text as UTF-8 internally, convert to UTF-16 just before calling W functions, and convert results back to UTF-8.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8

cards.q: What is a surrogate pair?
cards.a: Two UTF-16 units that together encode one code point above U+FFFF.
cards.lessonTitle: Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8

cards.q: What does the share mode in `CreateFileW` control?
cards.a: What other handles may do with the file (read, write, delete) while this handle is open.

cards.q: Where should a Windows game keep save files and settings?
cards.a: Save files under the user's Saved Games folder; settings, logs and caches under Local (or Roaming) AppData. Found with `SHGetKnownFolderPath`.

cards.q: When would you use the Windows file API instead of `std::fstream` and `std::filesystem`?
cards.a: When you need features the standard library does not expose, such as share modes, asynchronous I/O, memory-mapped files, change notifications or exact error codes.

cards.q: What is a window procedure?
cards.a: The callback function, registered with the window class, that Windows calls with every message for windows of that class.

cards.q: How does a message loop end?
cards.a: `PostQuitMessage` puts `WM_QUIT` in the queue; `GetMessageW` returns 0 when it reads it, ending the loop.

cards.q: How does a game's loop differ from a classic message loop?
cards.a: It uses `PeekMessageW` to handle every waiting message without blocking, then runs one frame of update and rendering, and repeats.

cards.q: What are the main steps of a Win32 program's start-up?
cards.a: Register a window class with a window procedure, create a window of that class, show it, then run the message loop.

cards.q: What is the client area of a window?
cards.a: The part inside the borders and title bar, where the program draws.

cards.q: What must you do with every GDI object you create?
cards.a: Delete it when finished, after deselecting it from any device context it was selected into.

cards.q: What is a virtual-key code?
cards.a: A number identifying a key independently of the keyboard layout, given in `wParam` of key messages; letter keys use their upper-case ASCII code.

cards.q: Where are a mouse message's coordinates, and in what coordinate system?
cards.a: Packed in `lParam`, x in the low 16 bits and y in the high 16 bits, both signed, relative to the window's client area.

cards.q: When should a game read input from messages and when from the current key state?
cards.a: Messages for discrete events such as a single press or typed text; the current state (or a state array kept from messages) for continuous actions such as holding a movement key.

cards.q: What is DLL search-order hijacking, and how do you prevent it?
cards.a: Getting a program to load a malicious DLL by placing it in a folder searched before the real one. Prevent it by restricting the search with `SetDefaultDllDirectories`, loading by full path, and keeping DLL folders unwritable by untrusted users.

cards.q: What is an `HMODULE`?
cards.a: The address at which a module (an exe or DLL) is loaded in the process; its headers start there.

cards.q: How can a program use a function that might not exist on the user's version of Windows?
cards.a: Look it up with `GetProcAddress` at run time and call it only if it was found, or delay-load the DLL that provides it.

cards.q: What are virtual terminal sequences?
cards.a: Strings starting with the escape character that the console interprets as commands, such as moving the cursor, changing colour or clearing the screen, instead of printing them.

cards.q: How does a console game read single key presses without blocking?
cards.a: It checks `GetNumberOfConsoleInputEvents`, then reads the waiting events with `ReadConsoleInputW` and handles key-down events by their virtual-key code.

cards.q: How can a windowed game show `std::cout` output during development?
cards.a: Call `AllocConsole` to create a console and reopen `stdout` on `CONOUT$`.

cards.q: What is the difference between a program, a process and a module?
cards.a: A program is an executable file; a process is a running instance with its own address space, threads and handles; a module is an exe or DLL mapped into a process.

cards.q: What does `CreateProcessW` give back, and what must you do with it?
cards.a: A process handle, a thread handle and their ids, in `PROCESS_INFORMATION`. Both handles must be closed.

cards.q: Why must arguments containing spaces be quoted?
cards.a: The command line is a single string that the new process splits on spaces, so quotes are needed to keep an argument with spaces together.

cards.q: How many bytes is a page on x64 Windows, and how many bits of an address are the offset within it?
cards.a: 4,096 bytes; the low 12 bits are the offset.

cards.q: What is a canonical address?
cards.a: One whose bits 48 to 63 are all copies of bit 47. Only canonical addresses are valid; user-mode ones are in the lower half, kernel ones in the upper half.

cards.q: What happens when a program touches a page that was paged out to disk?
cards.a: A page fault: the kernel reads the page back into a free frame, updates the page table, and resumes the program, which only notices a delay.

cards.q: What are the three states a page can be in?
cards.a: Free, reserved (addresses set aside, nothing behind them) and committed (backed by memory, accessible according to its protection).

cards.q: What is a guard page used for?
cards.a: An inaccessible page placed after a buffer or below a stack, so that running off the end faults immediately; for stacks, it also triggers committing more stack.

cards.q: Why reserve a large region and commit it gradually?
cards.a: The data never has to move as it grows, so pointers stay valid and nothing is copied, while unused space costs no memory.

cards.q: What three memory types does `VirtualQuery` report, and what is each?
cards.a: `MEM_IMAGE`, memory belonging to a loaded exe or DLL; `MEM_MAPPED`, a mapped file; `MEM_PRIVATE`, memory private to the process such as heaps, stacks and `VirtualAlloc` allocations.
cards.lessonTitle: Exploring Your Own Process with VirtualQuery

cards.q: Why does one DLL show up as several regions?
cards.a: Each of its sections has a different protection (code is execute-read, constants read-only, data read-write), and a region only covers pages with identical attributes.
cards.lessonTitle: Exploring Your Own Process with VirtualQuery

cards.q: How can a tool tell which module a code address belongs to?
cards.a: Query the address; if its type is `MEM_IMAGE`, its `AllocationBase` is the module's base address (`HMODULE`), which gives the module's name.
cards.lessonTitle: Exploring Your Own Process with VirtualQuery

cards.q: What is a context switch?
cards.a: The scheduler saving one thread's registers and loading another's, so the core continues with a different thread.

cards.q: Why do games use a fixed set of worker threads instead of creating a thread per task?
cards.a: Creating a thread is slow and uses a stack's worth of address space; reusing a few workers fed from a job queue avoids that cost.

cards.q: What must happen to a `std::thread` before it is destroyed?
cards.a: It must be joined or detached, or the program terminates.

cards.q: What is a data race?
cards.a: Two threads accessing the same memory at the same time, at least one of them writing, without synchronisation. In C++ it is undefined behaviour.

cards.q: Why should a mutex always be locked through an RAII guard?
cards.a: So it is released on every path out of the scope, including early returns and exceptions; a forgotten unlock freezes every other thread that needs it.

cards.q: How do you prevent deadlocks between two mutexes?
cards.a: Always lock them in the same order everywhere, or lock both together with `std::scoped_lock`.

cards.q: What two steps does the Tool Help API use?
cards.a: Take a snapshot with `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot`, then walk it with the matching First and Next functions.

cards.q: What does a module entry tell you?
cards.a: The module's name and path, its base address and its size in the process.

cards.q: Why can holding only a process id be risky?
cards.a: When the process ends, its id can be reused, so the id might later refer to a different process.

cards.q: What three things does the access check compare?
cards.a: The process's token (who it is, its groups and integrity), the object's security descriptor (who may do what), and the rights requested.
cards.lessonTitle: Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No

cards.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
cards.a: Requesting and holding only the rights the code actually needs, so that requests succeed for ordinary users and a compromised program can do less harm.
cards.lessonTitle: Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No

cards.q: What is a protected process?
cards.a: A process the kernel shields from other processes, even administrators: they cannot read its memory, inject code into it or debug it.
cards.lessonTitle: Access Rights, Tokens and Why Windows Says No

cards.q: What is ASLR and why does it exist?
cards.a: Address space layout randomisation loads modules, heaps and stacks at different addresses on each run, so attackers cannot rely on knowing where code or data is.
cards.lessonTitle: Address Space Layout Randomisation and Base Addresses

cards.q: What is an RVA?
cards.a: A relative virtual address: an offset from the start of a module, which stays the same wherever the module is loaded.
cards.lessonTitle: Address Space Layout Randomisation and Base Addresses

cards.q: What do relocations do?
cards.a: They list every absolute address stored inside a module, so the loader can adjust them when the module is loaded somewhere other than its preferred base.
cards.lessonTitle: Address Space Layout Randomisation and Base Addresses

cards.q: What is a register?
cards.a: A small, fixed storage location inside the processor, read and written without any memory access. x64 has sixteen general-purpose 64-bit ones.
cards.lessonTitle: Registers and the Shape of an Instruction

cards.q: What are `eax`, `ax` and `al`?
cards.a: The low 32, 16 and 8 bits of `rax`, usable as registers in their own right.
cards.lessonTitle: Registers and the Shape of an Instruction

cards.q: What three kinds of operand can an instruction have?
cards.a: A register, an immediate constant stored in the instruction, or a memory location whose address is computed from registers and constants.
cards.lessonTitle: Registers and the Shape of an Instruction

cards.q: What four parts can a memory operand's address have?
cards.a: A base register, an index register multiplied by 1, 2, 4 or 8, and a constant displacement.
cards.lessonTitle: Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes

cards.q: What is the difference between `movzx` and `movsx`?
cards.a: Both widen a small value; `movzx` fills the new bits with zeros (for unsigned types), `movsx` with copies of the sign bit (for signed types).
cards.lessonTitle: Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes

cards.q: What does `lea` do?
cards.a: It computes the address of a memory operand and stores that number, without accessing memory; compilers also use it for fast arithmetic.
cards.lessonTitle: Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes

cards.q: What is the difference between the carry flag and the overflow flag?
cards.a: CF is set when the result does not fit as an unsigned number; OF is set when it does not fit as a signed number.

cards.q: Why do compilers avoid `div`?
cards.a: Division is many times slower than other arithmetic, so division by constants is replaced with shifts, masks or multiplication by a precomputed constant.

cards.q: How is `x % 8` computed for unsigned `x`?
cards.a: With `and x, 7`: keeping the low three bits gives the remainder after dividing by 8.

cards.q: What do `cmp` and `test` compute, and what do they keep?
cards.a: `cmp` subtracts and `test` ANDs their operands; both keep only the flags and throw the result away.

cards.q: How can you tell from compiled code whether a comparison was signed or unsigned?
cards.a: From the jump or set instruction that reads the flags: `l`/`g` conditions are signed, `b`/`a` conditions unsigned.

cards.q: What do `setcc` and `cmovcc` do?
cards.a: `setcc` writes 1 or 0 into a byte depending on a condition; `cmovcc` copies a value only if the condition holds. Both avoid a branch.

cards.q: What do `push` and `pop` do to `rsp`?
cards.a: `push` subtracts 8 and then stores; `pop` loads and then adds 8.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack, push, pop, call and ret

cards.q: What are a function's prologue and epilogue?
cards.a: The instructions at its start that save registers and reserve its stack frame, and the matching ones at its end that release the frame and restore the registers before `ret`.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack, push, pop, call and ret

cards.q: Why can a stack buffer overrun make a program jump to a random address?
cards.a: The overrun can overwrite the return address stored above the locals, and `ret` then jumps to whatever value is there.
cards.lessonTitle: The Stack, push, pop, call and ret

cards.q: Which registers carry the first four arguments?
cards.a: `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9` for integers and pointers; `xmm0` to `xmm3` for floating point, by position.

cards.q: What is shadow space?
cards.a: 32 bytes the caller reserves on the stack above the return address, where the callee may store its four register arguments.

cards.q: What is the difference between volatile and non-volatile registers?
cards.a: A called function may overwrite volatile registers freely; it must preserve non-volatile ones, saving and restoring them if it uses them.

cards.q: What is a basic block?
cards.a: A straight run of instructions with one entry at the top and one exit at the bottom: no jumps in or out in between.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch

cards.q: How does a compiler implement `a && b`?
cards.a: As a chain of conditional jumps: if `a` is false, jump straight past the code that tests `b` and the body.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch

cards.q: What three parts make up a jump table's code?
cards.a: A range check (one unsigned compare and jump to default), a load of the case's target from a table indexed by the value, and an indirect jump to it.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch

cards.q: How does a member access appear in assembly?
cards.a: As a memory operand `[pointer + offset]` with a size such as `dword ptr`, where the offset is the member's position in the struct.
cards.lessonTitle: Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly

cards.q: How do you find the element size of an array of structs from compiled code?
cards.a: Look at how the index is scaled: a multiply or `lea` combination, times the addressing-mode scale, gives the struct size.
cards.lessonTitle: Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly

cards.q: What does a chain of dependent 8-byte loads represent?
cards.a: Following pointers through objects: each load reads a pointer member, which becomes the address for the next.
cards.lessonTitle: Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly

cards.q: What do the suffixes `ss`, `sd`, `ps` and `pd` mean?
cards.a: Scalar single, scalar double, packed single (four floats) and packed double (two doubles).

cards.q: Where do a function's float arguments and float result go on x64 Windows?
cards.a: The first four arguments in `xmm0` to `xmm3` by position; the result in `xmm0`.

cards.q: What does a loop need for the compiler to vectorise it?
cards.a: Independent iterations, no calls or complicated control flow in the body, and contiguous data, so several elements can be processed per instruction.

cards.q: How do you add an assembly file to a Visual Studio C++ project?
cards.a: Enable the masm build customisation for the project, add a `.asm` file, and make sure its item type is Microsoft Macro Assembler.

cards.q: What does an assembly function have to do with non-volatile registers?
cards.a: Save any it uses (for example with `push`) and restore them before returning.

cards.q: How do you check the stack is aligned at a call?
cards.a: Start from "8 off a multiple of 16" at entry and add up every push and `sub rsp`; at the call the total must make `rsp` a multiple of 16, with at least 32 bytes reserved for shadow space.

cards.q: Name five transformations an optimiser applies.
cards.a: Inlining, unrolling, vectorisation, branch removal with setcc/cmov, constant folding, strength reduction, tail calls, dead code elimination.

cards.q: Why can a breakpoint in a function fail to hit in a Release build?
cards.a: The function may have been inlined into its callers or removed, so there is no separate code at that location to stop in.

cards.q: What is the best first step when reading an unfamiliar optimised function?
cards.a: Find its structure (loops, calls and returns) before decoding individual arithmetic tricks.

cards.q: What are the steps of the debugging loop?
cards.a: Reproduce, observe precisely, form one specific hypothesis, test it with an experiment that could disprove it, and repeat until confirmed; then fix and check against the original reproduction.

cards.q: What is bisecting, and why is it so effective?
cards.a: Repeatedly splitting the search space in half and finding which half holds the bug; the number of steps grows only with the logarithm of the size.

cards.q: Why make a minimal reproduction?
cards.a: A tiny program showing the bug is much easier to reason about, often reveals the cause while shrinking it, and is what others need to help.

cards.q: What does a PDB contain?
cards.a: The names and address ranges of functions, line-number tables, types and layouts, local variables, and other data that lets a debugger map machine code back to source.

cards.q: Why must you keep the PDB of every build you release?
cards.a: A PDB matches only its own build; without it, crash reports from that build cannot be turned into function names and line numbers.

cards.q: What is a symbol server?
cards.a: A service that hands out the PDB matching a module's signature on request, such as Microsoft's server for Windows DLLs, or a studio's own for its builds.

cards.q: What is the difference between an assert and error handling?
cards.a: An assert checks something that can only be false if the code has a bug, and stops; error handling deals with things that can legitimately go wrong at run time, such as missing files or bad input.

cards.q: Why wrap a macro's body in `do { ... } while (false)`?
cards.a: So that the macro acts as a single statement and works correctly after an `if` or `else` without braces.

cards.q: What makes a log line useful?
cards.a: A level, a time stamp or frame number, a category, and concrete facts with the values involved.

cards.q: What is a crash dump?
cards.a: A file capturing a process's state at a moment (modules, threads, registers, stacks and some or all memory) that a debugger can open later.

cards.q: How does a program write its own minidump when it crashes?
cards.a: It installs an unhandled exception filter with `SetUnhandledExceptionFilter`, and in it calls `MiniDumpWriteDump` with the exception information.

cards.q: What do you need to turn a dump from a player into a readable call stack?
cards.a: The exact PDB files of the build the player was running.

cards.q: Why learn WinDbg when Visual Studio has a debugger?
cards.a: It analyses crash dumps quickly, works where Visual Studio is not installed, has deep Windows-specific commands, and is the debugger used for the kernel.

cards.q: What is the difference between commands starting with `.` and with `!`?
cards.a: `.` commands control the debugger itself; `!` commands are extensions provided by debugger DLLs.

cards.q: Which commands show locals, a typed structure and raw memory?
cards.a: `dv` for locals, `dt` for a typed structure, and `db`/`dd`/`dq` for memory as bytes, dwords or qwords.

cards.q: Which settings make a Release build debuggable without slowing it down?
cards.a: Generating a full PDB (`/Zi` and the linker's `/DEBUG`), plus `/Zo` for better variable locations.

cards.q: How do you see a value the debugger reports as optimised away?
cards.a: Find, in the disassembly, the register or stack slot the value was loaded into, and read it from the Registers or Watch window.

cards.q: Name three common causes of bugs that only appear in Release builds.
cards.a: Uninitialised variables, out-of-bounds accesses, data races, side effects inside asserts, timing differences, and undefined behaviour exploited by the optimiser.

cards.q: How do you find the threads involved in a deadlock?
cards.a: Break All, then look at every thread's stack for waits inside lock functions; for each, note the lock it waits for and the locks it holds, and find the cycle.

cards.q: What is the Parallel Stacks window good for?
cards.a: Seeing all threads' call stacks at once, with shared frames merged, to spot the unusual thread quickly.

cards.q: Why do races often disappear when you add logging?
cards.a: Logging changes the timing between threads, which changes whether the racing accesses overlap.

cards.q: What is the difference between sampling and instrumenting profilers?
cards.a: Sampling periodically records call stacks to find statistically where time goes, with no code changes; instrumenting records exact times of marked sections, giving per-frame timelines.
cards.lessonTitle: Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes

cards.q: What is the difference between self and total time?
cards.a: Self time is spent in the function's own instructions; total time includes everything it calls.
cards.lessonTitle: Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes

cards.q: How long is a frame at 60 frames per second?
cards.a: About 16.7 milliseconds.
cards.lessonTitle: Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes

cards.q: Name four legitimate uses of reverse engineering.
cards.a: Security research, malware analysis, interoperability with file formats and protocols, preservation of old software, debugging third-party code, and learning.
cards.lessonTitle: What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules

cards.q: What do reverse engineers recover, and what can they not recover?
cards.a: They recover the program's logic, control flow, strings, imports and often class names; they cannot recover comments, local names, most types or the original source.
cards.lessonTitle: What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules

cards.q: What should you do if you find a security vulnerability?
cards.a: Report it privately to the vendor and give them time to fix it before discussing it publicly.
cards.lessonTitle: What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules

cards.q: In what order do the parts of a PE file come?
cards.a: DOS header and stub, PE signature, file header, optional header (with data directories), section table, then the sections themselves.

cards.q: What does the section table tell you for each section?
cards.a: Its name, its RVA and size in memory, its offset and size in the file, and its flags (code, data, readable, writable, executable).

cards.q: Why should a PE parser check offsets against the file size?
cards.a: Malformed or malicious files can contain offsets and counts that point outside the file; using them unchecked reads out of bounds.

cards.q: What three things does an import descriptor point to?
cards.a: The DLL's name, the import lookup table (which functions, by name or ordinal) and the import address table (where the loader writes their addresses).

cards.q: How does `GetProcAddress` find a function by name?
cards.a: It binary-searches the export table's sorted name array, takes the corresponding ordinal index, and returns the module base plus that function's RVA.

cards.q: How do you convert an RVA to a file offset?
cards.a: Find the section containing the RVA, then compute RVA − the section's VirtualAddress + its PointerToRawData.

cards.q: What does Ghidra's automatic analysis do?
cards.a: It disassembles reachable code, identifies functions, follows cross-references, recognises standard library functions, and decompiles each function.

cards.q: Why does `main` not start at the entry point?
cards.a: The entry point is the C runtime's start-up code, which initialises the runtime and then calls `main`.

cards.q: What does annotating a program in a disassembler involve?
cards.a: Renaming functions and variables, creating struct types and applying them, and adding comments as you understand each part.

cards.q: What are signs that an address is the start of a function?
cards.a: It is the target of calls, it has a typical prologue, it is listed in the `.pdata` unwind table, or it follows padding after another function's return.

cards.q: What is an induction variable?
cards.a: The register or variable that changes by a fixed step each time round a loop and is compared with the limit; it shows what the loop iterates over.

cards.q: What is the most useful first step when reading an unknown function?
cards.a: Work out its signature: which argument registers it reads and what it returns, then look at what it calls.

cards.q: What can vtables tell you about an unknown program?
cards.a: Which polymorphic classes exist, which virtual functions each has (in order), which functions are overridden, and through constructors that reference them, which code creates objects of each class.

cards.q: What does RTTI provide to a reverse engineer?
cards.a: Class names (as decorated strings) and their inheritance relationships, linked from each vtable.

cards.q: How does a `strings`-style tool work?
cards.a: It scans the bytes for runs of printable characters, in single-byte and UTF-16 forms, at least a minimum length long, and lists them with their offsets.

cards.q: What does dynamic analysis add to static analysis?
cards.a: Real values, the actual targets of indirect calls, which branches are taken with real input, and the order things happen in.

cards.q: Why are API calls good breakpoints in an unknown program?
cards.a: They mark significant actions (files, network, memory, loading code), their arguments reveal what is happening, and stepping out finds the program's own code responsible.

cards.q: Where can you see whether a conditional jump will be taken, before stepping it?
cards.a: From the flags in the Registers window, or the debugger's own indication; x64dbg shows it on the jump instruction.

cards.q: What is a cross-reference?
cards.a: A recorded reference from one place in the program to another: a call, jump, read, write, address-taking or data pointer.
cards.lessonTitle: Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used

cards.q: How is the target of an `E8` call computed?
cards.a: Take the address of the next instruction (the call's address plus 5) and add the signed 32-bit displacement that follows `E8`.
cards.lessonTitle: Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used

cards.q: Why might static analysis miss a reference?
cards.a: The address may be computed at run time, looked up by name with `GetProcAddress`, or stored in a structure built while the program runs.
cards.lessonTitle: Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used

cards.q: What three pieces of evidence does each member access give?
cards.a: The member's offset, its size, and from the instruction and its use, clues to its type (float or integer, signed or unsigned, pointer or value).

cards.q: Why look at the code that creates the struct?
cards.a: The allocation gives the total size, and the constructor's initialisation shows members and their starting values, including any vptr.

cards.q: What should you do with members you are unsure about?
cards.a: Record them as unknown or guessed, with the evidence, and confirm them dynamically before relying on them.

cards.q: What is the routine for a practice target?
cards.a: Write it, build it optimised without symbols, analyse it statically and dynamically, write down conclusions, check against the source, then compare with the PDB loaded.

cards.q: How can you make a practice target easier or harder?
cards.a: Build it without optimisation for an easier version, or with whole-program optimisation (more inlining) and without RTTI for a harder one.

cards.q: Why do level 5 targets include a file the program wrote?
cards.a: Documenting a file format from the program and its data, then writing a compatible reader, is the core of interoperability work.

cards.q: What is a frame?
cards.a: One pass of the game loop: input processed, the world updated once, and one image rendered.

cards.q: Why keep input, update and render separate?
cards.a: So each can run at its own rate or on its own thread, input can be recorded and replayed, and rendering never changes the world.

cards.q: Why does the order of systems in the update matter?
cards.a: Later systems use earlier ones' results; running them out of order shows or uses stale data.

cards.q: What is the difference between a variable and a fixed time step?
cards.a: A variable step updates the simulation by however long the last frame took; a fixed step always updates by the same amount, running as many updates as real time requires.

cards.q: How does the accumulator work?
cards.a: Each frame adds the real elapsed time to it; while it holds at least one step, one update runs and the step is subtracted; the remainder carries over.

cards.q: Why interpolate when rendering?
cards.a: To draw smooth motion between fixed simulation steps when the display refreshes at a different rate.

cards.q: What are entities, components and systems?
cards.a: Entities are ids; components are plain data structs attached to entities; systems are functions that process every entity having a particular set of components.

cards.q: What problem with deep inheritance does ECS solve?
cards.a: Rigid hierarchies that cannot express new combinations of features without restructuring, and the scattered, virtual-call-heavy memory layout of individually allocated objects.

cards.q: What does a sparse set store, and why?
cards.a: A sparse array from entity id to dense index, plus dense arrays of entities and components, giving constant-time lookup, addition and removal and fast contiguous iteration.

cards.q: What are the main stages a triangle goes through on the GPU?
cards.a: The vertex shader transforms its vertices, rasterisation finds the pixels it covers, the pixel shader colours each, and output merging applies the depth test and blending.
cards.lessonTitle: A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline

cards.q: What coordinate spaces does a vertex pass through?
cards.a: Model space, world space, view (camera) space, clip space and finally screen space.
cards.lessonTitle: A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline

cards.q: What is the difference between being CPU-bound and GPU-bound in rendering?
cards.a: CPU-bound means the CPU cannot prepare and submit work fast enough (often too many draw calls); GPU-bound means the GPU cannot process the vertices and pixels fast enough.
cards.lessonTitle: A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline

cards.q: Why should game code use actions rather than keys?
cards.a: So controls can be rebound, several inputs can trigger the same action, and gamepads work without changing game logic.

cards.q: How are pressed and released worked out?
cards.a: By comparing each action's state in this frame's snapshot with the previous frame's: up then down is pressed, down then up is released.

cards.q: Why apply a 2D stick's dead zone to its length rather than to each axis?
cards.a: Per-axis dead zones distort diagonal directions and make movement snap to the axes.

cards.q: Why hand out handles instead of raw pointers to resources?
cards.a: Handles stay safe when resources are unloaded or reloaded, and make hot reloading possible.

cards.q: How does reference counting decide when to unload?
cards.a: Each acquire increments the resource's count and each release decrements it; when it reaches zero, no one uses it and it may be unloaded.

cards.q: How can a game load resources without freezing?
cards.a: Read and decode them on worker threads, hand the results back through a queue, and use placeholders or a loading screen until they are ready.

cards.q: What should a save contain, and what should be rebuilt?
cards.a: The minimal state that cannot be derived (player stats, inventory, world changes, choices); everything derived and all static level content is rebuilt on load.

cards.q: What goes in a save file's header?
cards.a: A magic number identifying the file type, a format version, the length of the data and a checksum.

cards.q: How do old saves keep working after the format changes?
cards.a: Each version has a loader, and older data is migrated step by step through each newer version to the current one.

cards.q: What belongs in C++ and what in data or scripts?
cards.a: Engine systems and performance-critical code in C++; content, balance numbers and one-off gameplay logic in data files and scripts.

cards.q: Why validate data files when loading?
cards.a: A mistake in data should produce a clear message naming the file, line and key immediately, not a confusing failure much later.

cards.q: What does registering a function with Lua do?
cards.a: It makes a C++ function callable from scripts under a given name, defining what scripts may do in the engine.

cards.q: What steps does the method follow?
cards.a: Build and run it, map the top-level folders, find the main loop, trace one feature end to end, match patterns to known ideas, and write it all down.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game

cards.q: How do you find the main loop?
cards.a: Start at the entry point and step through with the debugger, or search for it, until reaching the loop that runs once per frame.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game

cards.q: What should you check before reusing code from an open-source game?
cards.a: Its licence, and that your use follows the licence's terms.
cards.lessonTitle: Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game

cards.q: What three things happen each time round Delve's main loop?
cards.a: All waiting events are processed, the game is updated in fixed steps for the elapsed time, and the frame is rendered and presented.

cards.q: What does `SDL_RenderPresent` do?
cards.a: Shows the frame that has been drawn into the back buffer, swapping it to the screen, waiting for the monitor's refresh when vsync is on.

cards.q: Why does `main.cpp` own only the window, loop and timing?
cards.a: So the game state and rules live in `Game`, separate from platform code, keeping update and render apart and the logic testable.

cards.q: How is the map stored in memory?
cards.a: As one flat vector of tiles in row-major order, with the index of (x, y) being y × width + x.

cards.q: What does the level loader need to check?
cards.a: That all rows are the same width, every character is known, there is exactly one player start, and it should report problems with line numbers.

cards.q: How does a tile sheet make drawing more efficient?
cards.a: All tiles come from one shared texture, so the renderer can batch them instead of switching textures for every tile.

cards.q: What does "turn-based on a real-time loop" mean for Delve?
cards.a: The loop runs every frame for input and drawing, but the game rules advance only when the player acts; then every monster acts once.

cards.q: Which moves cost a turn?
cards.a: Moving onto floor or stairs, opening a door, and attacking; bumping into a wall or the edge does not.

cards.q: How does the renderer make tile-by-tile movement look smooth?
cards.a: It draws the player between the previous and current tiles, moving from one to the other over a short time after each move.

cards.q: What are a Delve monster's states, and what moves it between them?
cards.a: Idle, Chasing and Attacking: noticing the player starts a chase, being adjacent starts attacking, the player moving away resumes the chase, and losing the player for a while returns to idle.

cards.q: What is a distance map?
cards.a: A grid holding, for every reachable tile, the number of steps to a goal (here the player), built with one breadth-first search from the goal.

cards.q: How do monsters avoid moving onto the same tile?
cards.a: They act one at a time in a fixed order, checking whether the tile they want is free at the moment they move.

cards.q: What are the steps of the damage formula?
cards.a: Roll to hit against the attacker's accuracy; on a hit, damage is power minus half the armour plus a small random spread, at least 1; subtract it from the defender's health.

cards.q: What is the difference between an item definition and an item in the inventory?
cards.a: The definition is shared data (name, effects, stack limit) loaded from a file; an inventory slot holds only the definition's id and a count.

cards.q: In what order does picking up fill the inventory?
cards.a: First top up existing stacks of the same item to their limit, then use empty slots, and leave anything that does not fit.

cards.q: How does Delve divide its state for level transitions and saving?
cards.a: Into player state, which survives between floors, and floor state, which is discarded and rebuilt from the level file plus a record of changes.

cards.q: What does a Delve save contain?
cards.a: The floor number, opened doors, surviving monsters with position, health and state, items on the floor, the player's position, health, stats and inventory, and the random generator's state.

cards.q: How is the save written so a crash cannot destroy it?
cards.a: Built in memory, written with its header and checksum to a temporary file, flushed, then atomically swapped in, keeping the previous save as a backup.

cards.q: What does the console's registry store for each command?
cards.a: Its name, a one-line help text, and a handler function that takes the game and the arguments and returns a message.

cards.q: What should the game do with key presses while the console is open?
cards.a: Send them only to the console (text input, editing keys, history), not to the game's controls.

cards.q: How does command history recall work?
cards.a: Up moves back through previous commands, Down moves forward, and moving past the newest returns to the line being typed.

cards.q: What makes an action feel good to perform?
cards.a: Immediate, clear feedback: visual effects, motion and sound that confirm what happened, all done in presentation without changing the game state.

cards.q: What goes into a Delve release folder?
cards.a: The exe, the DLLs it needs, the data files, a readme, and the licences of the libraries used.

cards.q: What are the two ways to handle the Visual C++ runtime?
cards.a: Ship the Visual C++ Redistributable installer with the game, or build with `/MT` so the runtime is linked into the exe.

cards.q: Name three documented ways for a tool to get data from a game.
cards.a: Shared memory, named pipes or sockets, log files and ETW events, the debugging API for a process the tool starts, and crash dumps.
cards.lessonTitle: Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs

cards.q: Why is it best for the game to publish data deliberately?
cards.a: The layout is agreed and versioned, it needs no special rights, it is fast, and it keeps working when the game changes, unlike guessing at memory layouts.
cards.lessonTitle: Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs

cards.q: What may and may not go into a shared-memory block?
cards.a: Fixed-size plain data such as numbers and fixed arrays; never pointers or types that own heap memory.
cards.lessonTitle: Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs

cards.q: What are the three columns of a hex view?
cards.a: The address of the row, the bytes in hexadecimal, and the same bytes as text with non-printable bytes shown as dots.

cards.q: What rights does a tool need to read another process's memory?
cards.a: `PROCESS_VM_READ`, and `PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION` (or the limited form) to query regions; a process the tool created itself already comes with a full-access handle.

cards.q: How does `ReadProcessMemory` report a partial read?
cards.a: It returns failure and sets the number of bytes actually copied, which may be less than requested.

cards.q: What is the shape of a debugger's main loop?
cards.a: Wait for a debug event, inspect and handle it, then continue the debuggee with a status, until the process exits.
cards.lessonTitle: A Minimal Debugger of Your Own

cards.q: Name five kinds of debug event.
cards.a: Process creation, thread creation and exit, DLL load and unload, exceptions (including breakpoints), debug output strings, and process exit.
cards.lessonTitle: A Minimal Debugger of Your Own

cards.q: Why are out-of-process crash reporters built as debuggers?
cards.a: As the crashing program's debugger, they receive the second-chance exception with the program frozen at the fault and can write a dump from a healthy process.
cards.lessonTitle: A Minimal Debugger of Your Own

cards.q: What is a sequence lock's writer protocol?
cards.a: Increment the sequence (making it odd), write the data, increment it again (making it even).
cards.lessonTitle: A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State

cards.q: How does a reader know its copy is consistent?
cards.a: The sequence number was even before copying and unchanged after.
cards.lessonTitle: A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State

cards.q: Why does the telemetry block start with magic, version and size?
cards.a: So a tool can confirm it is looking at the right kind of data and knows which layout to use before trusting any field.
cards.lessonTitle: A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State

cards.q: What three connection states should a monitoring tool show?
cards.a: Connected and live, connected but stale (paused or frozen), and not connected (waiting for the game).
cards.lessonTitle: A Live Stats Panel for Your Game

cards.q: How does the tool find the game's telemetry?
cards.a: It lists running `delve.exe` processes, opens the mapping named with each one's process id read-only, and checks its header.
cards.lessonTitle: A Live Stats Panel for Your Game

cards.q: How does the panel draw without flickering?
cards.a: It builds the whole screen as one string starting with "cursor home" and writes it in a single call.
cards.lessonTitle: A Live Stats Panel for Your Game

cards.q: What does "append-only" mean for a shared layout?
cards.a: New fields are only ever added at the end, and existing fields are never moved, removed or changed in meaning.
cards.lessonTitle: Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools

cards.q: How does a reader use the size field?
cards.a: A field exists only if it lies entirely within the writer's size; the reader copies the smaller of the two sizes and treats the rest as unavailable.
cards.lessonTitle: Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools

cards.q: What are feature flags for?
cards.a: Saying which optional parts of the interface the writer currently provides, independent of the version.
cards.lessonTitle: Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools

cards.q: Why treat data from another process as untrusted?
cards.a: It may come from a different version, be half written, corrupted or buggy, so using it unchecked can crash the tool or show wrong values.

cards.q: Which waits in a tool need limits?
cards.a: All of them: retries of consistent reads, pipe reads, and connection attempts.

cards.q: What does "garbage testing" mean for a tool?
cards.a: Feeding its logic random, truncated, out-of-range and wrong-version data, and checking it reports problems without crashing.

cards.q: Name the layers through which a game can support mods.
cards.a: Data overrides, asset replacement, scripting, native plugins, and official editing tools.

cards.q: What is a mod conflict?
cards.a: Two mods changing the same file or entry, so that only the later one's change takes effect.

cards.q: What responsibilities come with supporting mods?
cards.a: Failing safely when a mod breaks, making native code obvious and trusted, recording mods in saves, and keeping anything that affects other players under server control.

cards.q: What is a virtual file system for mods?
cards.a: A layer over the real files that searches the enabled mods' folders, last first, before the base game, so mods can override any file by name.

cards.q: How does merging data from several mods work?
cards.a: Start from the base game's entries and apply each mod's entries in load order, overwriting only the keys that mod sets.

cards.q: What should happen when a mod's script has an error?
cards.a: The error is caught and reported with the mod's name, the mod is disabled, and the game carries on.

cards.q: What are the host API and the plugin API?
cards.a: The host API is the table of functions the game offers plugins; the plugin API is the table of functions every plugin provides so the game can initialise, update and shut it down.

cards.q: What may cross the plugin boundary?
cards.a: Integers, floats, plain fixed-size structs, UTF-8 `const char*` strings valid for the call, function pointers and opaque handles or ids.

cards.q: How should errors cross the boundary?
cards.a: As return codes; C++ exceptions must be caught on their own side and never propagate across.
